q: The term "diathesis" in the diathesis-stress model refers to:

concept.t: A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability that a person carries before the disorder appears; the Greek word means "disposition".
The stressor is the precipitant (trigger). Disorder develops when diathesis and enough stress combine; neither alone is usually sufficient.
In the "4 P" formulation, diathesis maps onto predisposing factors and stress onto precipitating factors.

wrong.a: That is the stressor, the precipitant or trigger; swapping it with the diathesis is the classic trap.
wrong.c: The person's reaction once stress arrives; coping can soften the outcome but is not the pre-existing vulnerability.
wrong.d: These come after an episode, whereas the diathesis is present before any disorder appears.

q: In Meehl's (1962) model, the inherited neural integrative defect is called:
who: Paul E. Meehl, APA presidential address (1962)

concept.t: Meehl proposed that an inherited schizogene produces schizotaxia, a subtle neural integrative defect: purely the inherited neurological vulnerability.
Through ordinary social learning, a schizotaxic person develops schizotypy, the personality organisation built on it. Only a minority of schizotypes decompensate into schizophrenia.
Schizotaxia = biology (neural defect); schizotypy = psychology (personality). Schizotypal personality disorder is a separate DSM category.

wrong.a: Meehl's name for the personality organisation (cognitive slippage, anhedonia, interpersonal aversiveness, ambivalence) learned on top of the defect; the near-identical name is the trap.
wrong.c: A DSM personality disorder category (detachment, restricted emotion), not one of the levels in Meehl's chain.
wrong.d: Echoes Langfeldt's schizophreniform states (acute onset, good prognosis), now a DSM duration category of 1 to 6 months; not an inherited defect.

q: "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia", which proposed that episodes are time-limited while vulnerability is enduring, was written by:

concept.t: Zubin and Spring (1977), in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology, restated diathesis-stress as the vulnerability-stress model, still the standard textbook diagram.
Vulnerability is the enduring trait. An episode occurs when stress pushes a person above their threshold and is time-limited, a challenge to Kraepelin's assumption of inevitable deterioration.
"Seven-seven": Zubin and Spring share 1977 with Engel's biopsychosocial model, but the two are different ideas.

wrong.a: Wrote "Schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia", the earlier APA address at the root of the model, not the vulnerability paper.
wrong.b: Popularised the phrase "diathesis-stress" in Genetic Theory and Abnormal Behavior, drawing on the Danish adoption studies; he did not write this paper.
wrong.d: Wrote the classic Psychological Bulletin review asking how diathesis and stress combine, focused on depression rather than schizophrenia.

q: Hammen's (1991) finding that depressed women experience more dependent, interpersonal stressful events is known as:

concept.t: Stress generation: people with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own stress, so they meet more dependent events, especially interpersonal conflicts.
They do not meet more independent events (outside their control, such as an earthquake). A dependent event is partly produced by the person, such as a breakup after repeated arguments.
It breaks the idea that stress just happens to the vulnerable person, one reason Monroe and Simons called for a dynamic model.

wrong.a: Robert Post's (1992) idea, borrowed from epilepsy research, that later mood episodes need less and less stress.
wrong.c: Pluess and Belsky (2013): some people benefit more than others from positive experiences, the positive pole of differential susceptibility.
wrong.d: Family criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement that predicts relapse in schizophrenia (Brown, Birley and Wing, 1972; Vaughn and Leff, 1976).

q: In the hopelessness theory of Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), the diathesis is:
who: Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), hopelessness theory

concept.t: The cognitive diathesis is a negative inferential (attributional) style: explaining negative events with stable and global causes, inferring negative consequences and negative things about oneself.
When such a person meets negative events they become hopeless, the proximal sufficient cause of "hopelessness depression". It is an explicit diathesis-stress theory (Psychological Review).
It revised the learned helplessness reformulation of Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale (1978).

wrong.a: A genetic candidate from Caspi et al. (2003), later not supported (Border et al., 2019); a gene, not a cognitive style.
wrong.c: A family-environment stressor that predicts relapse, mainly in schizophrenia; it is stress acting on the person, not their own diathesis.
wrong.d: Beck's (1983) personality diathesis of dependence on relationships, which leaves people vulnerable to interpersonal loss; a different theory.

q: The large 2019 study by Border and colleagues concluded that 5-HTTLPR x stress effects on depression:

concept.t: Caspi et al. (2003), using the Dunedin cohort, reported that short 5-HTTLPR alleles raised depression risk after stressful life events: the textbook G x E example.
Border et al. (2019), in the American Journal of Psychiatry, used very large samples and found no support for historical candidate gene or candidate G x E hypotheses.
Caspi is now a failed replication story (Risch 2009 was also negative); polygenic approaches have replaced single candidate genes.

wrong.a: The opposite of the finding: strong confirmation was Caspi's 2003 claim, which the large studies did not replicate.
wrong.b: A subgroup claim the study did not make; its headline was no support for the interaction.
wrong.d: Reverses the real pattern: stress itself strongly predicted depression (Risch 2009), while the gene x stress interaction did not hold.

q: A trait that predicts worse outcomes in adverse environments and better outcomes in supportive environments, compared with others, best fits:

concept.t: Differential susceptibility: some people are more plastic, so the same trait makes them do worse in adverse environments but better in supportive ones, "for better and for worse".
The susceptible line is steeper and crosses the other: a crossover (disordinal) interaction. Diathesis-stress gives only a fan-shaped ordinal one.
Belsky (1997) proposed it on evolutionary grounds; Belsky and Pluess (2009) reviewed the evidence in Psychological Bulletin.

wrong.a: "For worse" only: vulnerable people do worse under stress, but in a supportive environment they do no better than others.
wrong.c: Post's (1992) idea that later mood episodes need less stress; about recurrence, not environment quality.
wrong.d: Engel's (1977) general philosophy that biology, psychology and social context all matter; it makes no crossover prediction.

q: "Biological sensitivity to context" was proposed by:
who: W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce J. Ellis (2005)

concept.t: Boyce and Ellis (2005), in Development and Psychopathology, argued that high stress reactivity (autonomic and adrenocortical) reflects heightened sensitivity to context, both harmful and protective.
A U-shaped relation: highly reactive children are over-represented in both very stressful and very protective early environments.
Boyce later popularised the orchid vs dandelion metaphor in The Orchid and the Dandelion (2019).

wrong.a: Wrote "Beyond diathesis stress" in Psychological Bulletin, the review of differential susceptibility: a close cousin with a different label.
wrong.c: Reported the 5-HTTLPR x stress interaction in the Dunedin cohort, the classic gene x environment example.
wrong.d: Organised the forms of vulnerability-stress models (dichotomous, quasi-continuous, ipsative, threshold), not this idea.

q: Which component is NOT one of the classic dimensions of expressed emotion rated on the Camberwell Family Interview that predict relapse?

concept.t: Thought broadcasting (one's thoughts escape and are known to others) is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom in the patient, not an EE dimension.
Expressed emotion (EE) rates relatives' attitudes toward the patient; critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement predict relapse.
Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) showed it; Vaughn and Leff (1976) replicated it using the Camberwell Family Interview.

wrong.a: A core EE dimension: the relative's critical remarks about the patient, counted on the Camberwell Family Interview.
wrong.b: A core EE dimension: rejection of the patient as a person, beyond criticism of specific behaviour.
wrong.c: A core EE dimension: over-protective, self-sacrificing or exaggerated emotional responses by the relative.

q: Robert Post's (1992) kindling hypothesis proposes that in recurrent mood disorder:

concept.t: Post borrowed kindling from epilepsy research. First mood episodes are usually triggered by major life stress; later ones need less and less, and may occur almost spontaneously.
Earlier episodes sensitise the system, so the threshold for later episodes falls: the diathesis itself grows over time.
Monroe and Harkness (2005) split it into stress sensitisation (smaller stressors become enough) and stress autonomy (episodes occur without stress).

wrong.a: The exact reverse of kindling: the threshold falls, not rises, as episodes recur.
wrong.c: Wrong from the start: first episodes are usually triggered by major life stress.
wrong.d: Kindling says later episodes need little or no stress, so no particular kind of life event is required.

q: The term "schizophrenia" was first introduced by Eugen Bleuler in:
who: Eugen Bleuler, 1908 lecture (German Psychiatric Association, Berlin)

concept.t: Bleuler used the word in a 1908 lecture; the monograph, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien, followed in 1911 and the English translation (Joseph Zinkin) in 1950.
From Greek schizein (to split) and phren (mind): the splitting of thought, emotion and will from one another, not a split personality.
Read which event the question names: 1908 = word introduced, 1911 = monograph, 1950 = English edition.

wrong.a: Not a Bleuler date; 1899 is Kraepelin's 6th edition, which consolidated dementia praecox.
wrong.c: The year of the monograph Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien, not the first use of the word.
wrong.d: The English translation by Joseph Zinkin, and also the year of Schneider's Klinische Psychopathologie; far too late for the coinage.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of Bleuler's four A's?
who: Eugen Bleuler, fundamental vs accessory symptoms

concept.t: Associations, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism: a later teaching mnemonic for Bleuler's fundamental symptoms, present in every case and at every stage.
Hallucinations were accessory symptoms for Bleuler: they come and go and occur in other illnesses, so the diagnosis does not rest on them.

wrong.a: One of the four: contradictory feelings, wishes or thoughts toward the same object held at once; Bleuler coined the word.
wrong.b: One of the four: withdrawal from external reality into an inner world of fantasy; Bleuler coined this word too.
wrong.d: One of the four, and the central one: loosening of associations, the chief primary symptom in Bleuler's account.

q: Emil Kraepelin consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into dementia praecox in his:

concept.t: In the 6th edition (1899) Kraepelin consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into one disease, dementia praecox, sharing early onset and a deteriorating course.
In the same edition he set it against manic-depressive insanity, episodic with good recovery. This dichotomy still splits the schizophrenia and mood chapters of DSM and ICD.
The term appears in the 4th edition (1893), at first for a narrower group; the unified concept dates from the 6th.

wrong.a: Where the Latin term first appears, but only for a narrower group among the "degenerative" processes; not yet the unified concept.
wrong.c: Came well after the consolidation (the 8th edition ran 1909 to 1915) and added further subforms such as simple dementia praecox.
wrong.d: Bleuler's work, not Kraepelin's: the monograph that renamed the illness "the group of schizophrenias".

q: A patient reaches out to shake the doctor's hand, withdraws it, then extends it again, repeatedly. This is best described as:

concept.t: Ambitendency is the volitional form of Bleuler's ambivalence: wanting and not wanting to act at once, so the patient starts to shake hands, withdraws, then extends the hand again.
Bleuler also described affective ambivalence (loving and hating the same person) and intellectual ambivalence ("I am a man" and "I am not a man").
Ambivalence is the umbrella; ambitendency is also listed among catatonic motor signs in modern texts.

wrong.a: Automatic imitation of the examiner's movements, a catatonic sign; here the patient alternates their own action instead of copying.
wrong.c: A catatonic sign (catatonia was described by Kahlbaum) in which limbs stay where they are placed, with slight resistance like soft wax.
wrong.d: Sudden stopping of the train of thought, which Bleuler grouped with association disturbance; it affects thinking, not movement.

q: According to Bleuler, the primary symptom, a direct product of the disease process, was:
who: Eugen Bleuler, primary vs secondary symptoms

concept.t: Bleuler sorted symptoms twice: fundamental vs accessory (diagnostic) and primary vs secondary (causal). Primary means a direct product of the presumed organic disease process.
Loosening of associations was his chief primary symptom: both fundamental and primary, the core of the illness.
Autism was fundamental but largely secondary; delusions and hallucinations were accessory and secondary. Primary is not a synonym for fundamental.

wrong.a: Accessory and secondary: a psychological reaction to the primary disturbance, not its direct product.
wrong.b: Fundamental but largely secondary: present in every case, yet a psychological consequence of the loosening; the classic trap.
wrong.d: Accessory and secondary, like delusions; they often bring the patient to hospital but are not the core process.

q: Which of these is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom?

concept.t: Kurt Schneider listed 11 first-rank symptoms, easy to recognise and strongly suggestive of schizophrenia in the absence of organic brain disease.
Delusional perception: a normal percept is given a sudden, unconnected, self-referent delusional meaning. It is the only delusion among the FRS.
The first-rank voices are third-person: audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing the patient, and voices commenting on actions.

wrong.a: A second-rank symptom: it can support the diagnosis but is less specific and occurs in many disorders.
wrong.c: Also second rank; it belongs with Bleuler's affect disturbance and later negative symptoms, not Schneider's first-rank list.
wrong.d: Not first rank: Schneider's voices are third-person (arguing, discussing or commenting); command hallucinations in the second person do not qualify.

q: The term "autism" was coined by:

concept.t: Bleuler coined autism (Greek autos, self) for withdrawal into fantasy in schizophrenia, away from external reality; it is one of his four A's.
Kanner (1943) and Asperger (1944) borrowed it for a developmental condition of childhood, which is why one word now names two different disorders.

wrong.a: Borrowed the word in 1943 ("Autistic disturbances of affective contact") for a childhood developmental condition; he did not coin it.
wrong.b: Borrowed it in 1944 ("autistic psychopathy"); the trap is that his name is now tied to the childhood condition.
wrong.d: Unified dementia praecox (1899) and judged by course; he coined neither "schizophrenia" nor "autism", both Bleuler's words.

q: The US-UK Diagnostic Project (Cooper et al., 1972) showed that:
who: Cooper et al. (1972), US-UK Diagnostic Project

concept.t: New York hospital psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more often than London psychiatrists, including many patients London would have called manic-depressive or personality disordered.
With standardised assessment (the Present State Examination, PSE), most of the difference disappeared: the gap lay in diagnostic habits, not in the patients.
The US had adopted Bleuler's broad concept; Britain stayed closer to Kraepelin and Schneider. Findings like this pushed psychiatry toward operational criteria such as DSM-III (1980).

wrong.a: Most of the New York excess vanished under standardised rating, so it was a labelling difference, not more genuine illness.
wrong.c: The reverse: New York used the broader concept (Bleuler's influence), while London stayed closer to Kraepelin and Schneider.
wrong.d: Not a finding of the project; standardised rating showed broadly similar patients in both cities, with the difference lying in the labels.

q: In Timothy Crow's (1980) classification, Type II schizophrenia is characterised by:
who: Timothy Crow (1980), Type I vs Type II

concept.t: Type II: negative symptoms, chronic course, poor drug response, structural brain change (ventricular enlargement), intellectual impairment and poorer outcome.
Type I: positive symptoms, acute, good neuroleptic response, presumed dopamine (D2) excess, reversible, no intellectual impairment. Options (a) and (d) describe Type I.

wrong.a: Describes Type I: positive symptoms with good neuroleptic response and presumed D2 dopamine excess.
wrong.c: Acute, reversible illness fits Type I (or Langfeldt's good-prognosis schizophreniform states), not Type II's chronic course.
wrong.d: Also Type I: presumed dopamine excess with no intellectual impairment, whereas Type II includes intellectual impairment.

q: The long-term follow-up study at the Burghölzli showing that schizophrenia frequently does not run a uniformly deteriorating course was carried out by:

concept.t: Manfred Bleuler, Eugen's son and also director of the Burghölzli, personally followed a cohort (usually quoted as 208 patients) for over two decades; published in German in 1972, English in 1978.
The course was far less uniformly bad than Kraepelin held: a substantial minority recovered, many stabilised after the first years, and steady decline to severe end states was uncommon.
Do not confuse father and son: Eugen coined schizophrenia and autism; Manfred ran the long-term outcome study.

wrong.a: His father, who coined "schizophrenia" and "autism" and also directed the Burghölzli; the shared surname is the trap.
wrong.c: Norwegian psychiatrist (1939) who separated process schizophrenia from good-prognosis schizophreniform states.
wrong.d: Heidelberg psychiatrist who listed the 11 first-rank symptoms, a diagnostic contribution, not an outcome study.

q: The construct added by the theory of planned behaviour to the theory of reasoned action is:

concept.t: The theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975) works only for behaviours under full volitional control, where intending is enough to act.
Icek Ajzen added perceived behavioural control (PBC), how easy or hard the person thinks the act will be, to handle behaviours not under full volitional control.
TPB = TRA + PBC. The TPB is Ajzen's alone (1985 chapter, 1991 paper); Fishbein co-authored only the TRA.

wrong.a: Already in the TRA: perceived social pressure from important others, one of its two determinants of intention.
wrong.b: Already in the TRA as the immediate antecedent of behaviour; the TPB kept it rather than added it.
wrong.d: Not a construct of either theory: both use attitude toward the behaviour, not toward the object.

q: In TPB, the immediate antecedent of behaviour is:

concept.t: Intention is the person's readiness or plan to perform the act; it is the proximal determinant of behaviour in both the TRA and the TPB.
Attitude, subjective norm and PBC feed intention, which leads to behaviour. Memory hook: "A-S-P before I-B".
PBC may also act directly on behaviour, but only insofar as it mirrors actual control (skills, resources).

wrong.a: One step back: attitude toward the behaviour feeds intention, which then drives behaviour.
wrong.c: Two steps back: normative beliefs, weighted by motivation to comply, build the subjective norm.
wrong.d: Bandura's (1977) concept, which Ajzen called most compatible with PBC; it is not the TPB's proximal predictor.

q: Normative beliefs are weighted by:
who: Fishbein and Ajzen, theory of reasoned action (1975)

concept.t: Subjective norm = Σ normative belief × motivation to comply (SN = Σ njmj).
A normative belief is what a specific important other (a referent: parent, spouse, doctor) wants me to do; motivation to comply is how much I want to go along with that person.
Each construct is beliefs × weights, summed: behavioural beliefs × outcome evaluation, normative beliefs × motivation to comply, control beliefs × perceived power.

wrong.a: Weights behavioural beliefs to build attitude toward the behaviour (AB = Σ biei).
wrong.b: Weights control beliefs to build perceived behavioural control (PBC = Σ ckpk).
wrong.d: From Protection Motivation Theory (Rogers, 1975): the belief that the recommended action works, part of coping appraisal.

q: LaPiere's (1934) study is famous for showing:

concept.t: LaPiere toured the US (1930 to 1932) with a young Chinese couple; of about 251 establishments visited, only one refused them service.
About six months later, establishments that had served the Chinese couple were asked by letter; roughly 92% of replies said they would refuse Chinese guests, a stark attitude-behaviour gap.
Ajzen and Fishbein (1977) explained it with compatibility: a general attitude ("the Chinese race") cannot predict a specific act (serving this couple).

wrong.a: Festinger's dissonance theory; the classic forced-compliance study is Festinger and Carlsmith (1959).
wrong.c: Asch's line-judgement studies showed conformity to group pressure; LaPiere's study involved no group pressure.
wrong.d: Zajonc's finding (1968) that repeated exposure alone increases liking; unrelated to attitude-behaviour consistency.

q: The principle of compatibility requires attitude and behaviour to match on:
who: Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977), Psychological Bulletin

concept.t: An attitude predicts a behaviour well only when both are measured at the same level of specificity on TACT: Target, Action, Context, Time.
A general attitude toward religion will not predict attending a particular temple next Sunday, but it does predict an aggregate of religious behaviours.
Ajzen and Martin Fishbein first called it the principle of correspondence; Ajzen later relabelled it compatibility.

wrong.b: Dimensions describing the attitude itself (its direction and strength), not the four elements of a behaviour.
wrong.c: The classic tripartite (ABC) model of attitude components, not the elements of the behaviour.
wrong.d: Core constructs of the Health Belief Model (Hochbaum, Rosenstock and colleagues, 1950s).

q: PBC is expected to predict behaviour directly when:

concept.t: Perceived behavioural control (PBC) is how easy or hard a person thinks the behaviour will be. It is the one construct Ajzen added to the TRA.

PBC predicts behaviour directly, not only through intention, but only to the extent it accurately reflects actual control (real skills, resources, opportunities). The direct path works because PBC serves as a proxy for actual control.
When perceptions are unrealistic (little information, a new behaviour, changed circumstances) the direct path weakens.

wrong.a: The strength of the subjective norm bears on intention, not on the direct PBC path; what matters is how accurate PBC is, not how weak the other predictors are.
wrong.c: Fully volitional behaviour is the TRA's territory, where intending is enough to act; PBC was added for behaviours not under full volitional control.
wrong.d: Attitude valence is irrelevant here: attitudes feed intention, and whether they are positive or negative does not decide if PBC predicts behaviour directly.

q: Ajzen considered PBC most similar to:

concept.t: Ajzen explicitly linked PBC to Bandura's (1977) self-efficacy: beliefs in one's capability to organise and execute the courses of action required.
Ajzen distinguished PBC from generalised locus of control: PBC is about one specific behaviour, not a general expectancy that holds across situations.
PBC items split into two factors: self-efficacy (ease, confidence) and perceived controllability (whether it is up to me).

wrong.a: Julian Rotter's generalised expectancy of internal vs external control; the main trap, because Ajzen explicitly distinguished PBC from it.
wrong.c: Martin Seligman's passivity after repeated uncontrollable aversive events, a model of depression; not what Ajzen compared PBC to.
wrong.d: Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance (1957): tension from holding inconsistent cognitions; an attitude-change theory, unrelated to perceived control.

q: According to the commonly cited meta-analysis by Armitage and Conner (2001), TPB explains approximately what percentage of variance in behaviour?

concept.t: Armitage and Conner (2001), about 185 studies: the TPB explained about 27% of the variance in behaviour and about 39% in intention.
Behaviour sits further down the chain than intention, and the intention-behaviour gap cuts prediction. Self-reported behaviour was predicted better than objectively measured behaviour.
PBC added to the prediction of intention over attitude and subjective norm; subjective norm was the weakest predictor.

wrong.a: Too low; the TPB does far better than the weak attitude-behaviour link Wicker (1969) reported (typical correlation about .15, about 2% of variance).
wrong.c: The trap: 39% is the variance explained in intention, not behaviour, in the same meta-analysis.
wrong.d: Too high; neither figure in the meta-analysis comes close, intention at 39% or behaviour at 27%.

q: "If I finish dinner, then I will take my tablet immediately" is an example of:

concept.t: Peter Gollwitzer (1999) separated goal intentions ('I intend to do X') from implementation intentions: if-then plans that link a situation to a response.
The plan hands control to a situational cue (finishing dinner), so the act follows almost automatically. That is how if-then plans bridge the intention-behaviour gap.
The 'If X, then I will Y' wording is the giveaway.

wrong.a: What others actually do (Cialdini and colleagues, 1990), as in a littered car park making people litter; a social norm, not a personal plan.
wrong.b: A Health Belief Model construct: a trigger such as a symptom, reminder or media message that prompts action, not a self-made if-then plan.
wrong.d: A TPB belief about factors that help or hinder the behaviour (time, money, skill), feeding PBC; a belief, not a plan.

q: Which model includes "cues to action"?

concept.t: The Health Belief Model came from Hochbaum, Rosenstock and colleagues at the US Public Health Service in the 1950s, built to explain poor uptake of free tuberculosis X-ray screening.
Perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, plus cues to action; self-efficacy was added later (Rosenstock, Strecher and Becker, 1988).
Cues to action are a Health Belief Model construct, unique to the HBM. The HBM also has no intention construct.

wrong.a: Fishbein and Ajzen (1975): attitude toward the behaviour and subjective norm lead to intention; no cues to action.
wrong.b: Ajzen (1985, 1991): the TRA plus perceived behavioural control; still no cues to action.
wrong.d: Ronald Rogers (1975): threat appraisal and coping appraisal, built to explain fear appeals; no cues to action.

q: Which technique has the best temporal resolution?

concept.t: Temporal resolution is how precisely a method says when something happened. EEG records electrical activity directly, in milliseconds.
PET, fMRI and SPECT depend on slow haemodynamic or metabolic changes, because blood responds over seconds.
EEG is fast but poor at localisation (centimetres); fMRI localises better but is slow.

wrong.a: Tracer imaging of metabolism, blood flow or receptors; temporal resolution is poor, tens of seconds to minutes (FDG uptake takes about 30 to 45 minutes).
wrong.b: Best spatial resolution among non-invasive functional methods, but the BOLD response peaks about 4 to 6 s after activity, so it resolves seconds, not milliseconds.
wrong.d: Single-photon tracer imaging of blood flow; temporal resolution is poor (minutes), and spatial resolution is lower than PET.

q: The BOLD signal in fMRI depends mainly on the magnetic properties of:

concept.t: Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic: it distorts the local magnetic field and lowers the MR signal. Oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic and does not.
Active neurons draw more blood flow than the oxygen they use, so local deoxyhaemoglobin decreases and the BOLD signal rises.
fMRI measures blood oxygenation, an indirect index of neural activity, not neuronal firing.

wrong.a: Diamagnetic, so it barely affects the field; the trap is that it rises during activity, but the signal change comes from losing deoxyhaemoglobin.
wrong.c: Glucose metabolism is what FDG-PET measures; glucose plays no magnetic role in the BOLD signal.
wrong.d: An optional injected contrast agent for structural MRI; BOLD fMRI needs no injection and uses the blood's own haemoglobin.

q: The first clinical CT scan was performed by:

concept.t: Godfrey Hounsfield built the CT scanner at EMI. The first clinical brain scan was on 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, London, with radiologist James Ambrose.
Allan Cormack developed the mathematics (1963, 1964); Hounsfield and Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize.
A rotating X-ray beam measures attenuation from many angles and a computer rebuilds slices; brightness reflects tissue density.

wrong.a: Lauterbur published the first MR image using magnetic field gradients (1973), not a CT scan; he shared the 2003 Nobel with Peter Mansfield.
wrong.c: Moniz developed cerebral angiography in Lisbon (1927); his 1949 Nobel was for prefrontal leucotomy, not imaging.
wrong.d: Phelps helped develop the modern PET scanner at Washington University, St Louis (1973 to 1975), not CT.

q: On a T2-weighted MRI, cerebrospinal fluid appears:
who: MRI relaxation: T1 vs T2 weighting

concept.t: Hydrogen nuclei in water and fat are tipped by a radiofrequency pulse and relax at different rates, T1 and T2, depending on the tissue.
Water is bright on T2-weighted images, so CSF is bright, and so is most pathology (oedema, demyelination); that is why T2 is used to find lesions.
CSF is dark on T1 and on FLAIR, a T2-type image with the CSF signal suppressed. Hook: 'T2 = H2O bright'.

wrong.a: That is CSF on T1-weighted images and on FLAIR; the classic swap of the two weightings.
wrong.c: CSF always shows on MRI, bright or dark depending on weighting; no standard sequence makes it vanish.
wrong.d: Cortical bone has almost no mobile protons, so it is dark on both T1 and T2; CSF on T2 is the opposite, bright.

q: Which of the following involves no ionising radiation?
who: MRI physics: magnetic field and radio waves

concept.t: Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays) carries enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and can damage DNA.
MRI uses a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses, neither of them ionising. Its danger is metal (pacemakers, aneurysm clips), not radiation.

wrong.a: Builds slices from X-ray attenuation, and X-rays are ionising.
wrong.b: Injects a positron-emitting radioactive tracer whose annihilation gives gamma photons, so it is ionising.
wrong.c: Injects a gamma-emitting radioactive tracer (e.g. technetium-99m), so it involves ionising radiation.

q: Coincidence detection of two 511 keV photons is the basis of:
who: PET physics: positron annihilation, coincidence detection

concept.t: An injected tracer emits a positron, which travels about a millimetre, meets an electron and annihilates. Positron annihilation yields two 511 keV photons travelling in opposite directions.
A detector ring registers both photons at once (coincidence detection), and the computer places the source on the line between them.
FDG, a glucose analogue, gets trapped in active cells, so PET maps regional glucose metabolism.

wrong.a: Uses single photons and a rotating gamma camera: no positrons, no annihilation, no coincidence detection; the classic PET/SPECT swap.
wrong.c: Detects the tiny magnetic fields of neuronal currents with SQUID sensors; no tracer and no photons.
wrong.d: Measures X-ray attenuation from an external tube rotating around the head; the radiation does not come from a tracer inside the body.

q: Fractional anisotropy is a measure derived from:
who: Basser, Mattiello and Le Bihan, DTI (1994)

concept.t: Water diffuses more easily along axons than across them, because myelin and membranes restrict it. DTI measures the direction and degree of this diffusion in each voxel.
Fractional anisotropy (FA) runs from 0 (equal in all directions, as in CSF) to 1 (one direction only); it indexes directional water diffusion.
High FA means organised, intact white matter (e.g. corpus callosum); reduced FA is reported in many disorders.

wrong.a: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy gives a spectrum of chemical concentrations (NAA, choline, creatine) in a voxel, not diffusion direction.
wrong.c: Uses near-infrared light to estimate oxy- and deoxyhaemoglobin changes in outer cortex; it has no diffusion measure.
wrong.d: Event-related potentials are averaged EEG voltage changes time-locked to a stimulus (P300, N400); electrical, not white matter structure.

q: Which of these is NOT a neuroimaging technique?

concept.t: TMS (Anthony Barker and colleagues, Sheffield, 1985) uses a coil to send a brief magnetic pulse that induces current in the cortex, depolarising neurons.
It stimulates cortex rather than recording or imaging it; its research value is causal, a temporary virtual lesion.
TMS uses a magnet like MRI and MEG, but in a 'not neuroimaging' question TMS (or ECT, or tDCS) is the answer.

wrong.a: A real imaging method: magnetoencephalography records the tiny magnetic fields of neuronal currents with SQUID sensors, at millisecond resolution.
wrong.b: A real imaging method: near-infrared light estimates oxy- and deoxyhaemoglobin changes in outer cortex, a haemodynamic signal like fMRI.
wrong.d: A real imaging method: a gamma-emitting tracer and rotating gamma camera image regional cerebral blood flow.

q: The P300 component was first described by:

concept.t: The P300 (P3) is a positive ERP wave about 300 ms after a rare, task-relevant stimulus in an oddball paradigm; it reflects context updating.
Samuel Sutton, Margery Braren, Joseph Zubin and E. Roy John described it in 1965.
P300 amplitude is reduced in schizophrenia.

wrong.a: Kutas and Hillyard (1980) described the N400, a negativity about 400 ms after a semantically unexpected word ('warm bread with socks').
wrong.c: Näätänen and colleagues (1978) described the mismatch negativity (MMN), an automatic response to a deviant sound, even without attention.
wrong.d: Grey Walter and colleagues (1964) described the contingent negative variation (CNV), a slow negative shift between a warning and an imperative stimulus.

q: Enlarged lateral ventricles in schizophrenia were first demonstrated on CT by:
who: Johnstone, Crow, Frith and colleagues, The Lancet (1976)

concept.t: Eve Johnstone, Timothy Crow, Christopher Frith and colleagues (1976, The Lancet) showed on CT that chronic schizophrenia patients had larger lateral ventricles than controls.
It was the first CT demonstration and revived interest in brain structure in schizophrenia; pneumoencephalography studies from 1927 had only hinted at it.

wrong.b: Ingvar and Franzén (1974) described hypofrontality, reduced frontal blood flow in schizophrenia, using xenon-133 before PET; not ventricles, not CT.
wrong.c: Baxter and colleagues (1987) reported the OCD PET findings: orbitofrontal and caudate hypermetabolism that fell after successful treatment.
wrong.d: Raichle and colleagues (2001) named the default mode network, more active at rest; a functional finding, not a CT one.

q: Which type of defence mechanism is dissociation?

concept.t: George Vaillant (1977), working from the Harvard Grant Study, ranked defences into four levels: psychotic, immature, neurotic, mature.
Dissociation (neurotic denial) is neurotic, alongside repression, displacement, reaction formation and intellectualization: private distress, reality testing intact.
Dissociation is not immature, however dramatic dissociative disorders look. The DSM-IV Defensive Functioning Scale puts it at the mental inhibitions level, same neighbours.

wrong.a: The top level: altruism, humour, sublimation, suppression, anticipation, seen in healthy adults; dissociation is not among them.
wrong.b: Projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out; the trap, because dissociative disorders look dramatic.
wrong.d: Not one of Vaillant's levels; the one conscious defence, suppression, is classed as mature.

q: A technique in which a response that inhibits anxiety is paired with an anxiety-provoking stimulus, step by step, to break the conditioned link between that stimulus and anxiety is:

concept.t: Joseph Wolpe (1958): by reciprocal inhibition, a response incompatible with anxiety, made in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond. That is counterconditioning.
Relaxation training, an anxiety hierarchy rated on SUDS (0 to 100), then each scene imagined while relaxed, moving up only when calm. Systematic desensitization is this package.
'Gradual' plus 'relaxation' means desensitization. Reciprocal inhibition is the principle; systematic desensitization is the technique.

wrong.b: The most feared stimulus at full strength, no escape, until anxiety falls; works by extinction, not step-by-step pairing with relaxation.
wrong.c: Pairs the unwanted behaviour with an emetic or a shock to condition an aversion; it adds discomfort rather than inhibiting anxiety.
wrong.d: Meyer (1966), for OCD: face the obsession's trigger and block the compulsion; extinction, with no anxiety-inhibiting response paired in.

q: In habit reversal training (HRT), the technique used to make the person aware of the habit is:
who: Azrin and Nunn, habit reversal training (1973)

concept.t: Habit reversal training (Nathan Azrin and Gregory Nunn, 1973) treats tics and body-focused repetitive behaviours such as trichotillomania and nail biting.
Awareness training makes the person notice the habit: response description, response detection, early warning (the urge or first movement), situation awareness.
Competing response training, habit control motivation and generalization training complete the original four-phase package.

wrong.a: The next phase: a physically incompatible, inconspicuous action (clench fists for hair pulling) held until the urge passes; it replaces the habit rather than detecting it.
wrong.b: Part of habit control motivation in the original package (and of simplified HRT): others encourage the person; it motivates, it does not build awareness.
wrong.c: Rehearsing the routine across situations, often in imagination, so the skill transfers; not the awareness step.

q: The subjective confidence people have in their flashbulb memories is:
who: Neisser and Harsch (1992); Talarico and Rubin (2003)

concept.t: Flashbulb memories are vivid memories of where you were when you heard shocking news; Brown and Kulik (1977) coined the term.
Neisser and Harsch (1992, Challenger) found accuracy poor about 2.5 years on, confidence still high; Talarico and Rubin (2003, 9/11): 'confidence, not consistency'.
Emotional arousal at encoding plus heavy rehearsal make them vivid, so confidence is very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls.

wrong.a: The opposite: the shock makes these memories feel vivid and certain, so confidence is high, not low.
wrong.c: The core finding is a mismatch: confidence stays high while accuracy (consistency) falls like any memory.
wrong.d: The trap: accuracy falls but confidence does not follow it; Hirst and colleagues found confidence stayed high while consistency dropped.

q: An intervention in which the person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal is:

concept.t: Paradoxical intention (Viktor Frankl, first described 1939): the person intends or wishes for the feared thing, with humour, e.g. 'try to stay awake'.
Anticipatory anxiety, the fear of a symptom: wishing for the symptom removes the fear that feeds it.
'Doing the opposite of the goal to reach the goal' is paradoxical intention; 'stop watching yourself' is dereflection.

wrong.b: Frankl's other technique: turning attention away from yourself to a partner, task or meaning, for hyper-reflection; no wishing for the opposite.
wrong.c: Knight Dunlap (1932): performing the unwanted habit on purpose until fatigue; it repeats the habit itself rather than wishing for the opposite of a goal.
wrong.d: Wolpe's principle behind systematic desensitization: an anxiety-incompatible response weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond; a principle, not a paradoxical instruction.

q: In ICD-11, gender incongruence is placed in:

concept.t: In ICD-11, gender incongruence (HA60 adolescence or adulthood, HA61 childhood) is in Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health.
It is no longer framed as a mental disorder and needs no distress, but the code was kept for access to care. ICD-10 had gender identity disorders (F64) in Chapter V.
Relocated, not deleted. ICD-11 says gender incongruence; DSM-5 says gender dysphoria.

wrong.a: The mental disorders chapter, its old home in ICD-10 (Chapter V, F64); ICD-11 moved it out, though paraphilic disorders stayed in Chapter 6.
wrong.b: A distractor: gender incongruence concerns identity, not hormones, and moved to the sexual health chapter, not the endocrine one.
wrong.d: The trap: it was relocated, not deleted; the code was kept for access to care.

q: Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is:
who: Samkhya and the Bhagavad Gita: the three gunas

concept.t: In Samkhya and the Bhagavad Gita, prakriti (matter including the mind) is made of three gunas: sattva (clarity), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia); the dominant one shapes the person.
Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia (dull, lethargic, withdrawn), mapping to depression. Bavisha, jobless, not eating and unable to act, is in shutdown: tamas alone.
Stressed and racing would be rajas; stuck and inert is tamas.

wrong.a: Yama is the first limb of Patanjali's yoga (ethical restraints such as ahimsa, satya), not a guna or a state of mind.
wrong.c: Fails because yama is a limb of yoga, not a guna, so it cannot pair with tamas as her state.
wrong.d: Activity and passion (restless, craving, angry; maps to anxiety, agitation); 'stressed' tempts, but she is inert, not racing.

q: Which of the eight limbs of yoga is concentration, directing the mind's energy to a single point?

concept.t: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras list eight limbs (ashtanga): yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi.
Dharana, the sixth limb, is concentration: binding the mind to one point (3.1). It opens the three inner limbs.
Senses in is pratyahara; mind fixed on one point is dharana; focus flowing on its own is dhyana.

wrong.a: The fifth limb, withdrawal of the senses (2.54), the step just before concentration.
wrong.b: Not a limb: jnana yoga is the path of knowledge in the Gita, alongside karma and bhakti.
wrong.c: The seventh limb, meditation: an unbroken flow of that focus (3.2); dharana comes first, dhyana continues it.

q: Kegel exercises strengthen which part of the body?

concept.t: Arnold Kegel, an American gynaecologist, introduced the exercises in 1948 for urinary incontinence after childbirth.
They strengthen the pelvic floor, mainly the levator ani and its pubococcygeus (PC) part, which runs from pubic bone to tailbone and supports the bladder, bowel and uterus.
Squeeze and lift for a few seconds, relax, repeat in sets; used for stress urinary incontinence, postpartum recovery and prolapse.

wrong.a: Worked by core exercises such as crunches or planks; squeezing the abdomen is not a Kegel.
wrong.c: Worked by back-extension exercises; Kegels do not involve the lumbar spine.
wrong.d: Squeezing the buttocks is a common mistake, not a Kegel; the PC muscle lies deeper, in the pelvic floor.
